It is important to maintain a list of all products you use, including prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, and herbal supplements, and share this information with your doctor and pharmacist. Certain drugs may reduce the effectiveness of hormonal birth control by decreasing the levels of birth control hormones in your body, which can lead to pregnancy. Examples of such drugs include griseofulvin, modafinil, rifamycins (e.g., rifampin, rifabutin), ritonavir, and St. John’s Wort. Inform your doctor when starting any new medication and discuss whether you should use a reliable backup method of birth control. This medication may interfere with certain laboratory tests, such as those measuring sex-hormone-binding globulin or thyroid function, potentially causing inaccurate test results. Overdose: If this implant is swallowed, it may be harmful. If someone swallows it and experiences serious symptoms such as fainting or difficulty breathing, call 911 immediately. Uses: This product is a small, thin plastic rod inserted under the skin to prevent pregnancy. The rod gradually releases etonogestrel into the body over a three-year period. Etonogestrel is similar to a natural hormone produced by the body. This medication may be less effective in women who are significantly overweight or those taking certain medications (refer to the Drug Interactions section). How to Use: Read the patient information leaflet provided by your pharmacist or healthcare provider before the rod is inserted. Ask your doctor about the best time to schedule your appointment for insertion. Your doctor may require a pregnancy test before the procedure. The medication typically begins working immediately if the rod is inserted within the first five days of your menstrual period. If the rod is inserted at another time in your cycle, you may need to use a non-hormonal form of birth control (e.g., condoms, diaphragm, spermicide) for the first seven days after insertion. The rod will be inserted under the skin of your upper arm by a healthcare professional, usually in the arm you do not use for writing. Two bandages will cover the insertion site. Leave the top bandage on for 24 hours and the smaller bandage on as directed by your doctor, typically for three to five days. The rod must be removed after three years and can be replaced if continued birth control is desired. Side Effects: Common side effects may include nausea, stomach cramping or bloating, dizziness, headache, breast tenderness, acne, hair loss, weight gain, and vaginal irritation or discharge. Pain, bruising, numbness, infection, and scarring may occur at the insertion site. Menstrual periods may become irregular, with changes in timing, duration, or flow (e.g., heavier or lighter). Spotting between periods is also common, especially during the first few months of use. If bleeding is prolonged (lasting more than eight days) or unusually heavy, contact your doctor. Remember, this medication has been prescribed because your doctor has determined that the benefits outweigh the risks of side effects. Rarely, individuals using this medication have experienced serious, potentially fatal complications from blood clots (e.g., heart attack, stroke, or clots in the lungs, legs, or eyes). Severe allergic reactions to this drug are rare. This is not a complete list of possible side effects. In the U.S., contact your doctor for medical advice about side effects. In Canada, consult your doctor for medical advice regarding side effects. Precautions: Before using etonogestrel, inform your doctor or pharmacist if you are allergic to it, other progestins (e.g., norethindrone, desogestrel), anesthetics, antiseptics used during the procedure, or if you have any other allergies. This product may contain inactive ingredients that could cause allergic reactions or other issues. This medication may cause dizziness. Alcohol or marijuana (cannabis) can exacerbate this effect. Avoid driving, operating machinery, or performing tasks requiring alertness until you can do so safely. Limit alcoholic beverages. Limit time in the sun and avoid tanning booths and sunlamps. If you are nearsighted or wear contact lenses, you may experience vision problems or difficulty wearing your lenses. This product must not be used during pregnancy. If you become pregnant or suspect you may be pregnant, inform your doctor immediately. This medication passes into breast milk.
